notes.summary: This chapter covers sets and their operations (Venn diagrams, power sets, inclusion–exclusion), relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, equivalence) and functions (domain, range, one-one and onto, composition, inverse, periodicity, greatest integer function). JEE Main asks counting of relations and functions, domain and range of real functions, classification of given relations, and composition or functional-equation problems.
keyPoints: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets and 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets; P(P(A)) has 2^(2ⁿ) elements (16 when n = 2).
Three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(C ∩ A) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).
If n(A) = m and n(B) = n: relations from A to B = 2^(mn); functions from A to B = nᵐ; one-one functions = ⁿPₘ (m ≤ n); bijections (m = n) = n!.
On a set with n elements: all relations 2^(n²), reflexive 2^(n² − n), symmetric 2^(n(n + 1)/2), reflexive and symmetric 2^(n(n − 1)/2).
Equivalence relation = reflexive + symmetric + transitive; its equivalence classes split the set into disjoint parts (congruence mod 5 on Z gives 5 classes).
Domain rules: √g needs g ≥ 0, log g needs g > 0, 1/g needs g ≠ 0. Example: √(log₁₀((5x − x²)/4)) has domain [1, 4].
(f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)); in general f∘g ≠ g∘f. Only a bijection has an inverse; find f⁻¹ by solving y = f(x) for x.
Greatest integer function: [x] = n ⇔ n ≤ x < n + 1, so equations in [x] give intervals, e.g. [x] = 2 means 2 ≤ x < 3.
Periods: sin x and cos x → 2π; tan x, |sin x|, |cos x| → π; |sin x| + |cos x| → π/2.
Functional equations involving f(1/x) or f(−x): substitute to get a second equation and solve the two simultaneously.
traps: Mixing up the number of relations (2^(mn)) with the number of functions (nᵐ), or functions from A to B (nᵐ) with B to A (mⁿ).
Forgetting to add back n(A ∩ B ∩ C) in three-set inclusion–exclusion.
Checking only that a log's argument is positive when the log itself sits under a square root (the log must also be ≥ 0).
Treating [x] = k as the single point x = k instead of the interval [k, k + 1).
Declaring a relation symmetric or transitive after checking only a few pairs — one counterexample is enough to fail.
notes.examTip: In counting questions, write the formula in terms of n(A) and n(B) before substituting — most wrong options in JEE Main are the values of the neighbouring formulas.

questions.text: If a set A has exactly 2 elements, then the number of elements in P(P(A)), the power set of the power set of A, is:
questions.explanation:
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
P(A) has 2² = 4 elements.
P(P(A)) is the power set of a 4-element set, so it has 2⁴ = 16 elements.

questions.text: The number of one-one (injective) functions from a set with 3 elements to a set with 5 elements is:
questions.explanation:
Images must be distinct.
The first element has 5 choices, the second 4, the third 3.
Number = 5 × 4 × 3 = ⁵P₃ = 60.
(125 = 5³ counts all functions; 10 = ⁵C₃ ignores order.)

questions.text: If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 3, the total number of relations from A to B is:
questions.explanation:
A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B.
n(A × B) = 3 × 3 = 9.
Number of subsets = 2⁹ = 512.
(27 = 3³ is the number of functions from A to B.)

questions.text: The domain of the real function f(x) = √(log₁₀((5x − x²)/4)) is:
questions.explanation:
The square root needs log₁₀((5x − x²)/4) ≥ 0, i.e. (5x − x²)/4 ≥ 1.
5x − x² ≥ 4, so x² − 5x + 4 ≤ 0, i.e. (x − 1)(x − 4) ≤ 0.
This gives 1 ≤ x ≤ 4; on this interval the log's argument is ≥ 1, so it is automatically positive.
Domain = [1, 4]. ((0, 5) only makes the log defined.)

options: Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) are all in R — yes.
Symmetric: (1, 2) is in R but (2, 1) is not — no.
Transitive: the only chains are (1, 1),(1, 2) → (1, 2) and (1, 2),(2, 2) → (1, 2), both in R — yes.
So R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric.

questions.text: The number of symmetric relations that can be defined on a set with 4 elements is:
questions.explanation:
In a symmetric relation, each diagonal pair (a, a) can be chosen freely: 4 choices of in/out.
Each off-diagonal pair {(a, b), (b, a)} must be taken together: ⁴C₂ = 6 such blocks.
Number = 2^(4 + 6) = 2¹⁰ = 1024, matching 2^(n(n + 1)/2) with n = 4.
(4096 = 2¹² is the number of reflexive relations; 65536 = 2¹⁶ counts all relations.)

questions.text: Let f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1 for all real x. The values of x for which (f∘g)(x) = (g∘f)(x) are:
The set of all real x satisfying [x]² − 5[x] + 6 = 0, where [x] denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x, is:
questions.explanation:
Treat [x] as the unknown: ([x] − 2)([x] − 3) = 0, so [x] = 2 or [x] = 3.
[x] = 2 means 2 ≤ x < 3; [x] = 3 means 3 ≤ x < 4.
Union: 2 ≤ x < 4, i.e. x ∈ [2, 4).

questions.text: In a survey of 100 students, 50 study Physics, 45 study Chemistry and 40 study Mathematics; 20 study both Physics and Chemistry, 15 study both Chemistry and Mathematics, 18 study both Physics and Mathematics, and 10 study all three subjects. The number of students who study none of the three subjects is:
questions.explanation:
n(P ∪ C ∪ M) = n(P) + n(C) + n(M) − n(P ∩ C) − n(C ∩ M) − n(P ∩ M) + n(P ∩ C ∩ M).
= 50 + 45 + 40 − 20 − 15 − 18 + 10 = 92.
Students studying none = 100 − 92 = 8.
(18 results from forgetting to add back the 10 who study all three.)

questions.text: If a function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every real x ≠ 0, then f(2) equals:
The fundamental period of the function f(x) = |sin x| + |cos x| is:
questions.explanation:
f(x + π/2) = |sin(x + π/2)| + |cos(x + π/2)| = |cos x| + |sin x| = f(x), so π/2 is a period.
No smaller period exists: f² = 1 + |sin 2x|, so f(0) = 1 while f(x) > 1 for 0 < x < π/2.
Thus f first returns to the value 1 at x = π/2.
Fundamental period = π/2.
